facts.statement: Segnosaurus lived in southeastern Mongolia during the Late Cretaceous period, approximately 102 to 86 million years ago.
facts.quote: Segnosaurus is a genus of therizinosaurid dinosaur that lived in what is now southeastern Mongolia during the Late Cretaceous, about 102–86 million years ago.

facts.statement: Multiple incomplete but well-preserved specimens of Segnosaurus were discovered in the Gobi Desert in the 1970s, leading to its formal description in 1979.
facts.quote: Multiple incomplete but well-preserved specimens were discovered in the Gobi Desert in the 1970s, and in 1979 the genus and species Segnosaurus galbinensis were named.

facts.statement: A joint Soviet-Mongolian expedition discovered the partial skeleton of Segnosaurus at the Amtgay locality in the Bayan Shireh Formation in 1973.
facts.quote: In 1973, a joint Soviet–Mongolian expedition investigating the Bayan Shireh Formation at the Amtgay locality in the Gobi Desert of southeastern Mongolia discovered fossils that included the partial skeleton of an unknown dinosaur.

facts.statement: The genus and species Segnosaurus galbinensis were named by paleontologist Altangerel Perle in 1979.
facts.quote: These fossils were scientifically described in 1979 by the paleontologist Altangerel Perle, who named the new genus and species Segnosaurus galbiensis.

facts.statement: The name Segnosaurus means "slow lizard," and the species name galbinensis refers to the Galbin region.
facts.quote: The generic name Segnosaurus means "slow lizard" and the specific name galbinensis refers to the Galbin region.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus was estimated to be about 6 to 7 meters long and weigh approximately 1.3 metric tons.
facts.quote: Segnosaurus was a large-bodied therizinosaur that is estimated to have been about 6–7 m long and to have weighed about 1.3 MT.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus was a bipedal dinosaur with its body trunk tilted upwards.
facts.quote: It would have been bipedal, with the trunk of its body tilted upwards.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus had a small head with a beak at the jaw tips and a long, slender neck.
facts.quote: The head was small with a beak at the tip of the jaws, and the neck was long and slender.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus possessed robust forelimbs with three fingers bearing large claws and feet with four toes, a trait unique among theropods.
facts.quote: The forelimbs were robust and had three fingers which bore large claws, and the feet had four toes supporting the foot—apart from therizinosaurs, all theropods had three-toed feet.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus and its relatives were likely slow-moving, mainly herbivorous animals, contrasting with the carnivorous nature of most other theropods.
facts.quote: Segnosaurus and its relatives are thought to have been slow-moving animals that, as indicated by their unusual features, were mainly herbivorous, whereas most other theropod groups were carnivorous.

facts.statement: Therizinosaurs like Segnosaurus likely used their long forelimbs, necks, and beaks for browsing and had large guts to process plant material.
facts.quote: Therizinosaurs probably used their long forelimbs, long necks, and beaks when browsing, and large guts for processing food.

facts.statement: Research confirmed that the family Segnosauridae is a junior synonym of the family Therizinosauridae.
facts.quote: The new fossils also showed Segnosauridae was a junior synonym of the earlier named family Therizinosauridae.

facts.statement: A 2020 study by Campione and Evans estimated Segnosaurus body mass at 4.17 metric tons.
facts.quote: Campione & Evans in 2020, however, calculated its body mass at 4.17 MT.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus had a small head featuring a rhamphotheca, or horny beak, at the jaw tips and a long, slender neck.
facts.quote: The head would have been small with a rhamphotheca (horny beak) at the tip of the jaws, and a long, slender neck.

facts.statement: Fossils of basal therizinosaur genera like Beipiaosaurus and Jianchangosaurus show that these dinosaurs had simple, primitive feathers.
facts.quote: Therizinosaurs are known to have had simple, primitive feathers as evidenced by fossils of the basal (or "primitive") genera Beipiaosaurus—the second-known non-bird dinosaur preserved with such integuments after Sinosauropteryx—and Jianchangosaurus.

facts.statement: In 1991, Minoru Tamura and colleagues assigned Late Cretaceous fossils from Japan to Allosaurus, suggesting it was the youngest known representative of that genus.
facts.quote: In 1991, the paleontologist Minoru Tamura and colleagues reported vertebrae, limb bones, and teeth from the Late Cretaceous Jobu Formation of Kumamoto, Japan, which they assigned to Allosaurus sp. (of unspecified species), which would make it the youngest representative of that genus.

facts.statement: In 2025, André Burigo and Octávio Mateus reassigned previously identified Japanese fossils to Segnosaurus sp. based on femur similarities and the presence of other therizinosaur remains at the site.
facts.quote: The paleontologists André Burigo and Octávio Mateus instead found the femur similar to that of to Segnosaurus in 2025, and noted that other therizinosaur remains were known from the site, and they therefore reassigned these remains to Segnosaurus sp.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus had a down-turned lower jaw with teeth featuring additional denticles and third cutting edges on some hindmost teeth.
facts.quote: The lower jaw was down-turned at the front and the teeth were distinct in having additional denticles as well as third cutting edges in some of the hindmost teeth.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus possessed a backward-turned pubic bone, a feature shared only with birds and their closest dinosaurian relatives.
facts.quote: The pubic bone was turned backwards, a feature that is only seen in birds and the dinosaurs most closely related to them.

facts.statement: The nearly complete right half of Segnosaurus's lower jaw measures 379 mm in length, 55.5 mm in height, and 24.5 mm in depth.
facts.quote: The nearly complete right hemimandible (half of the mandible) is 379 mm long from front to back, 55.5 mm at the highest point, and 24.5 mm at the lowest.

facts.statement: The front part of Segnosaurus's lower jaw is deflected downwards at a unique 30-degree angle.
facts.quote: The front-most part of the dentary was strongly deflected downwards at about a 30-degree angle, a unique feature for this genus.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus is distinct among therizinosaurs because the very back of its lower jaw had no teeth.
facts.quote: Segnosaurus was distinct among therizinosaurs in that the hindmost part of the dentary was toothless.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus had 24 tooth sockets in its lower jaw, with teeth restricted to the front two-thirds, unlike Erlikosaurus which had 31 sockets.
facts.quote: The teeth were restricted to the front two-thirds of the dentary, which bore 24 alveoli (tooth sockets) in a manner similar to Jianchangosaurus but different from Erlikosaurus, in which nearly the entire dentary was toothed, bearing 31 alveoli.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus possesses the fewest lower jaw teeth (24 per side) and the largest teeth known among therizinosaurs.
facts.quote: Segnosaurus had the fewest teeth in the dentary; 24 in each half determined from the number of sockets, as well as the largest teeth known among therizinosaurs.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus's teeth were leaf-shaped with enlarged, tall, sideways-compressed crowns that slightly curved at the tips.
facts.quote: The dentary teeth were foliodont (leaf-shaped) and bore enlarged, relatively tall, sideways compressed crowns with a slight recurvature at the upper margin of the tips.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus is unique among all known theropods for having triple cutting edges (carinae) on its teeth.
facts.quote: Segnosaurus was unique among all known theropods in possessing triple carinae.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus's teeth had large, bulbous serrations with approximately 5 to 6 per 3 mm along the edges.
facts.quote: The denticles (serrations) were large and bulbous, diminishing slightly in size towards the tooth tips, with about 5–6 denticles per 3 mm.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus replaced its teeth in waves moving from the back to the front of the jaws, involving two to three new teeth at a time.
facts.quote: Segnosaurus replaced its teeth in waves running from back to front of the jaws, that encompassed two to three erupting crowns.

facts.statement: A pathological bone growth walled over the 14th tooth socket in Segnosaurus's right lower jaw, though the damage to the teeth prevents determining the specific cause.
facts.quote: The 14th alveolus on the right dentary of the holotype is walled over by seemingly pathological (due to injury or disease) bone growth but the teeth in that part of the dentary are damaged so it is not possible to determine how the teeth were affected by this.

facts.statement: While split tooth edges are usually considered abnormalities in other theropods, in Segnosaurus this feature was uniform and likely served a functional purpose rather than being a defect.
facts.quote: Such split carinae are known from other tetanuran theropods, where they are considered abnormalities caused by trauma, aberrant tooth replacement, or genetic factors. Though the condition in Segnosaurus was similar, it was uniformly expressed across the teeth of both dentaries, and does not appear to have been an abnormality, but served to roughen the contacts between tooth bases.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus had a massive humerus measuring 560 mm in length with an almost-cylindrical shaft.
facts.quote: The massive humerus was 560 mm in length; it had an almost-cylindrical shaft and well-defined condyles for articulation with the radius and ulna of the lower arm.

facts.statement: The radius of Segnosaurus was massive, measuring about 60 percent of the length of the humerus.
facts.quote: The radius was also massive—about 60 percent of the humerus—with a straight shaft.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus possessed an ulna that was thicker than the radius and approximately 70 percent the length of the humerus.
facts.quote: The ulna was thicker than the radius and slightly longer—about 70 percent of the humerus—and slightly twisted along its middle axis.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus had a three-fingered hand.
facts.quote: The hand was tridactyl (three-fingered).

facts.statement: The third finger claw of Segnosaurus was quite flat from top to bottom, a feature that may be unique to the species.
facts.quote: The ungual of the third finger was somewhat longer than the second phalanx and quite flat from top to bottom, which may have been a unique feature of Segnosaurus.

facts.statement: The pelvis of Segnosaurus was robust and featured sharply sideways-directed lobes at the front.
facts.quote: The pelvis of Segnosaurus was robust and had sharply sideways-directed lobes at the front.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus had a straight femur with an oval cross-section measuring 840 mm in length.
facts.quote: The femur was straight with an oval cross-section and was 840 mm in length.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus had a short, massive metatarsus consisting of five bones, with four functioning as support elements ending in four toes.
facts.quote: The metatarsus of the foot was short, massive, and consisted of five bones—four of which functioned as support elements and terminated in four toes.

facts.statement: Functionally four-toed feet were unique to derived therizinosaurs like Segnosaurus, distinguishing them from basal therizinosaurs and other theropods which had three-toed feet.
facts.quote: Functionally tetradactyl (four-toed) feet were unique to derived therizinosaurs; basal therizinosaurs and all other theropods had tridactyl feet in which the first toe was short and did not reach the ground.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus is distinctively characterized by hypertrophied (enlarged) epiphyses on the upper metatarsals.
facts.quote: The epiphyses on the upper metatarsals were hypertrophied (enlarged), a distinctive feature of the genus.

facts.statement: The sacrum of Segnosaurus consisted of six firmly fused vertebrae with broadened and elongated centra that were slightly longer than they were wide.
facts.quote: The sacrum consisted of six, firmly fused vertebrae; the centra of these vertebrae were broadened and relatively elongated, and each centrum was slightly longer than their width.

facts.statement: The forelimb elements of Therizinosaurus were originally misidentified as belonging to a giant turtle in 1954.
facts.quote: the forelimb elements of Therizinosaurus itself were originally identified as belonging to a giant turtle when described in 1954

facts.statement: In 1979, Perle proposed the new family Segnosauridae for Segnosaurus fossils.
facts.quote: In 1979, Perle noted the Segnosaurus fossils were possibly representative of a new family of dinosaurs, which he named Segnosauridae

facts.statement: Barsbold and Perle named the theropod infraorder Segnosauria in 1980, which contained only the family Segnosauridae.
facts.quote: In 1980, Barsbold and Perle named the new theropod infraorder Segnosauria, containing only Segnosauridae

facts.statement: In 1983, Barsbold kept Segnosaurus and Erlikosaurus within the family Segnosauridae.
facts.quote: Barsbold retained Segnosaurus and Erlikosaurus in the family Segnosauridae in 1983

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul argued in 1984 that segnosaurs were derived prosauropods rather than theropods.
facts.quote: Gregory S. Paul concluded in 1984 that segnosaurs had no theropodan features but were derived, late-surviving Cretaceous prosauropods

facts.statement: David B. Norman described Gregory S. Paul's hypothesis about segnosaurs as contentious in 1985.
facts.quote: David B. Norman considered Paul's idea contentious and "bound to provoke much argument" in 1985

facts.statement: Segnosaurians shared an opisthopubic pelvis, a slender mandible, and toothless front jaws.
facts.quote: they were united by their opisthopubic pelvis, slender mandible, and the toothless front of their jaws

facts.statement: Barsbold suggested segnosaurids were either a major deviation within theropods or possibly outside the group entirely.
facts.quote: Barsbold found that segnosaurids were so peculiar compared to more typical theropods that they were either a very significant deviation in theropod evolution, or were possibly outside the group

facts.statement: In 1983, Barsbold noted that segnosaurian ilia were similar to sauropods while their pelvis deviated from the theropod norm.
facts.quote: Later in 1983, Barsbold stated the segnosaurian pelvis deviated significantly from the theropod norm and found the configuration of their ilia generally similar to those of sauropods

facts.statement: Gregory S. Paul noted segnosaurs shared snout, mandible, and hindfoot traits with prosauropods, and cheek, palate, pubis, and ankle traits with ornithischians.
facts.quote: He found segnosaurs to be similar to prosauropods in the morphology of their snout, mandible, and hindfoot; to ornithischians in their cheek, palate, pubis, and ankle

facts.statement: In 1994, Perle and colleagues accepted the synonymy of Segnosauridae with Therizinosauridae and classified therizinosaurs as maniraptoran theropods related to modern birds.
facts.quote: Perle and his co-authors of a 1994 redescription of Erlikosauruss skull accepted the synonymy of Segnosauridae with Therizinosauridae and they considered therizinosaurs to have been maniraptoran theropods, the group that also includes modern birds

facts.statement: In 1995, Lev A. Nessov debated the theropod classification of therizinosaurs, arguing instead that they were a distinct group within Saurischia.
facts.quote: In 1995, Lev A. Nessov rejected the idea therizinosaurs were theropods; he considered them a distinct group within Saurischia.

facts.statement: The placement of Therizinosauria within Maniraptora remains debated, with studies ranging from grouping with oviraptorosaurs to being the most basal clade within Maniraptora.
facts.quote: The placement of Therizinosauria within Maniraptora continued to be unclear; in 2017, Alan H. Turner and colleagues found them to group with oviraptorosaurs while in 2009 Zanno and colleagues found them to be the most basal clade within Maniraptora, bracketed by Ornithomimosauria and Alvarezsauridae.

facts.statement: Zanno identified the inaccessibility, damage, and scarcity of cranial remains as significant obstacles to resolving evolutionary relationships within Therizinosauria.
facts.quote: She cited the inaccessibility, damage, potential loss of holotype specimens, scarcity of cranial remains, and fragmentary specimens with few overlapping elements as the most significant obstacles to resolving the evolutionary relationships within the group.

facts.statement: The presence of Nothronychus in North America during the Turonian stage suggests a faunal interchange between North America and Asia via a late-Early Cretaceous land bridge.
facts.quote: The presence of the derived therizinosaurid Nothronychus, which was most-closely related to Asian genera, in North America during the Turonian stage of the early Late Cretaceous also shows there would have been a faunal interchange between North America and Asia via a late-Early Cretaceous land bridge before that (during the Aptian/Albian), which is also seen in some other dinosaur groups.

facts.statement: Research from 1979 and 1981 suggested that Segnosaurus was not adapted for rapid movement due to its short, massive metatarsus and large, splayed toes.
facts.quote: In 1979 and 1981, Barsbold and Perle said the short, massive metatarsus and unusually large, splayed toes indicated that Segnosaurus and its relatives were not adapted for rapid locomotion

facts.statement: Researchers Barsbold and Perle hypothesized that Segnosaurus and its relatives might have been amphibious.
facts.quote: Barsbold and Perle suggested they could have been amphibious

facts.statement: A 1990 study by Barsbold and Maryańska concluded that Segnosaurus was a slow-moving animal based on its short, broad feet and bulky trunk.
facts.quote: Barsbold and Maryańska agreed in 1990 the short, broad feet and bulky trunks of the group indicated they were slow-moving animals

facts.statement: In 1993, Russell determined that previous skeletal restorations of therizinosaurs were inaccurate and that their arms were held off the ground.
facts.quote: Russell concluded in 1993 that Paul's skeletal restoration was inaccurate and that the arms of therizinosaurs were held clear off the ground

facts.statement: Nessov proposed in 1995 that therizinosaur claws were used for defense and that juveniles might have used them for climbing trees like sloths.
facts.quote: In 1995, Nessov suggested the elongated claws of therizinosaurs were used for defense against predators and that their young could have used their claws for arboreal locomotion along trunks and in tree crowns

facts.statement: A 2012 study found that therizinosaurs possessed well-developed senses of smell, hearing, and balance.
facts.quote: In a 2012 study of the endocranial anatomy of Erlikosaurus and other therizinosaurs that preserve braincases, Stephan Lautenschlager and colleagues found these dinosaurs had well-developed senses of smell, hearing, and balance

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that the smell and hearing of therizinosaurs may have aided in foraging, avoiding predators, and social interactions.
facts.quote: The former two senses may have played a role in foraging, predator evasion, and social behavior

facts.statement: A 2014 study concluded that therizinosaur hand claws were not used for digging.
facts.quote: In a 2014 study of the function of therizinosaur hand claws, Lautenschlager found that these would not have been used for digging

facts.statement: It remains debated whether therizinosaur hand claws were used for defense, combat, grasping trees, sexual display, or mating.
facts.quote: He could neither confirm nor disregard that the hand claws could have been used for defense, combat, stabilization by grasping tree trunks during high browsing, sexual display, or gripping mates during copulation

facts.statement: Martin Kundrát and colleagues identified dinosaur eggs from the Nanchao Formation in China as belonging to therizinosaurs in 2007.
facts.quote: Dinosaur eggs with embryos of the Dendroolithidae type from the Nanchao Formation of China were identified as belonging to therizinosaurs and described by Martin Kundrát and colleagues in 2007

facts.statement: Evidence suggests therizinosaur hatchlings were precocial and capable of leaving their nests to feed independently.
facts.quote: The development of the embryos and the fact that no adults were found in association with the nests indicate that therizinosaur hatchlings were precocial (capable of locomotion from birth) and able to leave their nests to feed alone, independently of their parents

facts.statement: Yoshitsugu Kobayashi and colleagues reported a theropod nesting ground in Mongolia in 2013 containing at least 17 egg clutches.
facts.quote: In a 2013 conference abstract, Yoshitsugu Kobayashi and colleagues reported a nesting ground of theropod dinosaurs from the Javkhlant Formation of Mongolia that contained at least 17 egg clutches within an area 22 x

facts.statement: Therizinosaur eggs found in Mongolia were spherical with rough surfaces, arranged in a circular cluster of eight eggs with no central opening.
facts.quote: Each clutch contained eight spherical eggs with rough surfaces; the eggs were in contact with each other and arranged in a circular structure with no central opening

facts.statement: The presence of multiple egg clutches suggests that some therizinosaurs nested colonially.
facts.quote: The multiple clutches indicate some therizinosaurs were colonial nesters like hadrosaurs, prosauropods, titanosaurs, and birds

facts.statement: Researchers suggest therizinosaurs nested at specific sites only once and did not return to them for subsequent breeding.
facts.quote: The eggs were found in a single stratigraphic layer, suggesting the dinosaurs nested at the site on a single occasion and did not exhibit site fidelity

facts.statement: Researchers Barsbold and Perle noted in 1979 and 1980 that therizinosaurs likely evolved in a different direction from typical predatory theropods.
facts.quote: Barsbold and Perle pointed out in 1979 and 1980 that their peculiar features probably reflected a different evolutionary direction than those of more typical theropods, many of which were considered effective, active predators.

facts.statement: In 1983, Barsbold speculated that Segnosaurus shifted to herbivory based on its horny beak and weakened teeth, features common in herbivorous dinosaurs but not carnivorous theropods.
facts.quote: In 1983, Barsbold said the horny beak at the front of the jaws and weakened teeth at the back were common features among herbivorous dinosaurs but not of carnivorous theropods, and speculated this might indicate segnosaurs had shifted to herbivory.

facts.statement: In 1984, Paul suggested therizinosaurs were herbivores because their skulls resembled prosauropods and ornithischians, featuring beaks, inset teeth, and jaw shelves indicating cheeks.
facts.quote: In 1984, Paul suggested they were herbivorous due to the similarities of their skulls to those of prosauropod and ornithischian dinosaurs, which include horny beaks, inset rows of teeth, and a shelf at the side of the jaws that indicated the presence of cheeks.

facts.statement: In 1985, Norman proposed that Segnosaurus might have been an aquatic fish-eater to explain its small teeth and broad feet, though he found the horny beak mysterious in that context.
facts.quote: Norman stated in 1985 the possibility Segnosaurus was an aquatic fish-eater could explain its small, pointed teeth and broad and perhaps webbed feet, but found it mysterious why it should have a horny beak.

facts.statement: In 1993 and 1997, Russell suggested therizinosaurs sat on their pelvises and used their long arms and flexible necks to browse leaves from trees and bushes.
facts.quote: In 1993 and 1997, Russell suggested therizinosaurs would have "sat" on their pelvises and supported their bodies on their hind limbs while using their long arms, claws, and flexible necks to reach leaves from trees and bushes with their beaks.

facts.statement: Russell suggested therizinosaurs browsed on riparian bushes and trees because their fossils are often found in river and lake sediments.
facts.quote: Because therizinosaur remains are often found in sediments deposited in river and lake environments, Russell said they may have browsed on riparian bushes and trees.

facts.statement: In 1995, Nessov suggested therizinosaurs in the Bissekty Formation of Uzbekistan fed indirectly on aquatic ecosystems by eating wasps that consumed carrion.
facts.quote: Based on the assemblage of fossils in the Bissekty Formation of Uzbekistan, Nessov suggested in 1995 that therizinosaurs could have been part of its nutrient-rich aquatic ecosystems, though perhaps indirectly, by feeding on wasps which had themselves fed on carrion of aquatic vertebrates.

facts.statement: In 2009, Zanno and colleagues identified therizinosaurs as the most widely accepted herbivorous theropods based on specific anatomical features.
facts.quote: In 2009, Zanno and colleagues stated therizinosaurs were the most-widely regarded candidates for herbivory among theropods and listed features associated with this diet.

facts.statement: In 2014, Lautenschlager found that therizinosaur hands could not reach vegetation pulled down by their arms if the neck was too short, suggesting they pulled lower branches to access higher foliage.
facts.quote: Lautenschlager found in 2014 the hands of therizinosaurs would have had to be able to extend the range of the animal to a point that could not be reached by the head if they were used for browsing and pulling down vegetation.

facts.statement: There is no direct evidence of therizinosaur diet, leading to multiple debated interpretations of their feeding behavior.
facts.quote: The unusual features of therizinosaurs have led to several interpretations of their feeding behavior; there is no direct evidence of their diet, such as stomach contents and feeding traces.

facts.statement: Norman debated in 1985 whether Segnosaurus was an aquatic fish-eater, noting the mystery of its horny beak in that context.
facts.quote: Norman stated in 1985 the possibility Segnosaurus was an aquatic fish-eater could explain its small, pointed teeth and broad and perhaps webbed feet, but found it mysterious why it should have a horny beak.

facts.statement: Zanno and colleagues debated whether herbivory in basal maniraptorans evolved independently multiple times or if it was a primitive condition.
facts.quote: Zanno and colleagues found the clades at the base of Maniraptora—Ornithomimosauria, Therizinosauria, and Oviraptorosauria—had either direct or morphological evidence for herbivory, which would mean either this diet evolved independently multiple times in coelurosaurian theropods or that the primitive condition of the group was at least facultative herbivory with carnivory only emerging in more derived maniraptorans.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus possessed unique dentary teeth with additional carinae and folded carinae featuring denticulated front edges.
facts.quote: Zanno and colleagues identified novel, complex features in the dentary teeth of Segnosaurus, including the presence of additional carinae and folded carinae with denticulated front edges

facts.statement: Segnosaurus had a higher relative bite force than Erlikosaurus, allowing it to feed on tougher vegetation.
facts.quote: Difference in relative bite force between the sympatric Segnosaurus and Erlikosaurus show the former would have been able to feed on tougher vegetation

facts.statement: Digital simulations indicate Segnosaurus dentaries experienced very low stress magnitudes during feeding.
facts.quote: Lautenschlager found the dentaries of Segnosaurus experienced one of the lowest stress magnitudes during extrinsic feeding scenarios

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Segnosaurus likely used a downwards-pulling head motion to grip vegetation rather than sideways or upwards movements.
facts.quote: A downwards-pulling motion of the head while gripping vegetation was more likely than a sideways or upwards movement

facts.statement: Segnosaurus fossils date to between 102 and 86 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: Fossils of Segnosaurus have been recovered from the Bayan Shireh Formation in Mongolia, which has been dated to about 102–86 million years ago during the Cenomanian to Turonian stages of the Late Cretaceous period

facts.quote: El pubis se volvió hacia atrás, una característica que solo se ve en las aves y los dinosaurios más estrechamente relacionados con ellas.

facts.statement: Segnosaurus was likely an omnivore or herbivore, possessing herbivorous traits such as an elongated neck, small skull, and a horny beak.
facts.quote: Generalmente se acepta que los tericinosáuridos fueron omnívoros o herbívoros, Mostrando características herbívoras como cuellos alargados, tamaño reducido del cráneo, ampliación de la cavidad de la pelvis, reducción de la fuerza de mordida, reducción de la musculatura del cráneo, La pérdida de dientes anteriores, el desarrollo de una rhamphotheca y una porción anterior del dentario

facts.statement: Researchers Barsbold and Perle suggested in 1979 and 1981 that Segnosaurus was not adapted for fast locomotion due to its short, massive metatarsals and unusually large extended toes.
facts.quote: En 1979 y 1981, Barsbold y Perle dijeron que el metatarso corto y masivo y los dedos extendidos inusualmente grandes indicaban que Segnosaurus y sus parientes no estaban adaptados para la locomoción rápida

facts.statement: In 1990, Barsbold and Maryańska agreed that the short, wide legs and bulky bodies of the group indicated they were slow-moving animals.
facts.quote: Barsbold y Maryańska acordaron en 1990 que las patas cortas y anchas y los troncos voluminosos del grupo indicaban que eran animales de movimiento lento

facts.statement: In 1995, Nessov hypothesized that the long claws of therizinosaurs were used for defense and that their young might have used them for arboreal locomotion.
facts.quote: En 1995, Nessov sugirió que las garras alargadas de los terizinosaurios se usaban para defenderse de los depredadores y que sus crías podrían haber usado sus garras para la locomoción arbórea

facts.statement: A 2012 study by Stephan Lautenschlager and colleagues found that therizinosaurs had well-developed senses of smell, hearing, and balance.
facts.quote: En un estudio de 2012 de la anatomía endocraneal de Erlikosaurus y otros terizinosaurios que preservan las cajas cerebrales, Stephan Lautenschlager y sus colegas encontraron que estos dinosaurios tenían sentidos del olfato, el oído y el equilibrio bien desarrollados

facts.statement: In a 2014 study, Lautenschlager concluded that the hand claws of therizinosaurs were not used for digging.
facts.quote: En un estudio de 2014 sobre la función de las garras de las manos de los terizinosaurios, Lautenschlager descubrió que estas no se habrían utilizado para cavar

facts.statement: In 2007, Martin Kundrát and colleagues identified dinosaur eggs with embryos of the type Dendroolithidae from China's Nanchao Formation as belonging to therizinosaurs.
facts.quote: Los huevos de dinosaurio con embriones del tipo Dendroolithidae de la Formación Nanchao de China fueron identificados como pertenecientes a terizinosaurios y descritos por Martin Kundrát y sus colegas en 2007

facts.statement: The therizinosaur eggs were arranged in a circular structure without a central opening, touching each other.
facts.quote: Los huevos estaban en contacto entre sí y dispuestos en una estructura circular sin abertura central

facts.statement: Multiple nesting sites indicate that some therizinosaurs nested colonially, similar to hadrosaurs, prosauropods, titanosaurs, and birds.
facts.quote: Las múltiples nidadas indican que algunos terizinosaurios anidaban coloniales como hadrosáuridos, prosaurópodos, titanosaurianos y aves

facts.statement: Fossils of Segnosaurus have been recovered from the Bayan Shireh Formation in Mongolia, dating to approximately 102–86 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Se han recuperado fósiles de Segnosaurus de la Formación Bayan Shireh en Mongolia, que data de hace unos 102-86 millones de años durante las etapas Cenomaniense a Turoniense del período Cretácico Tardío

facts.statement: The sediments of these formations were deposited by meandering rivers and lakes on an alluvial plain with a semi-arid climate.
facts.quote: Los sedimentos de estas formaciones fueron depositados por ríos serpenteantes y lagos en una llanura aluvial,terreno llano formado por sedimentos depositados por ríos de la sierra, con un clima semiárido

facts.statement: Therizinosaurs were the most abundant theropods in the Bayan Shireh Formation in terms of biodiversity.
facts.quote: Los terizinosaurios fueron los terópodos más abundantes en la Formación Bayan Shireh en términos de biodiversidad

facts.statement: Other dinosaurs found in the same formation included the ankylosaurid Talarurus, the hadrosaurid Gobihadros, the sauropod Erketu, and the ceratopsian Graciliceratops.
facts.quote: Otros dinosaurios incluyeron el anquilosáurido Talarurus, el hadrosáurido Gobihadros, el saurópodo Erketu, y el ceratopsiano Graciliceratops

facts.statement: The formation is distinguished by its variety and abundance of turtles, while invertebrates include ostracods and freshwater mollusks.
facts.quote: La formación se distingue por su variedad y abundancia de tortugas, y los invertebrados incluyen ostrácodos y moluscos de agua dulce

facts.statement: In 1970, Anatoly K. Rozhdestvensky suggested that Therizinosaurus used its large claws to open termite mounds or collect tree fruits.
facts.quote: En 1970, Anatoly K. Rozhdestvensky sugirió que Therizinosaurus, el único miembro del grupo conocido en ese momento, usaba sus grandes garras para abrir montículos de termitas o recolectar frutos de los árboles

facts.statement: In 1979 and 1980, Barsbold and Perle noted that the group's peculiar features likely reflected an evolutionary direction different from typical active and effective theropod predators.
facts.quote: Barsbold y Perle señalaron en 1979 y 1980 que sus características peculiares probablemente reflejaban una dirección evolutiva diferente a la de los terópodos más típicos, muchos de los cuales se consideraban depredadores activos y efectivos

facts.statement: In 1984, Paul suggested they were herbivores due to skull similarities with prosauropods and ornithischians, including horny beaks, rows of inserted teeth, and a jaw shelf indicating cheek presence.
facts.quote: En 1984, Paul sugirió que eran herbívoros debido a las similitudes de sus cráneos con los de los dinosaurios prosaurópodos y ornitisquios, que incluyen picos córneos, filas de dientes insertados y un estante al lado de las mandíbulas que indica la presencia de mejillas

facts.statement: In 1985, Norman proposed that Segnosaurus might have been an aquatic fish-eater to explain its small, pointed teeth and wide, possibly webbed feet.
facts.quote: Norman declaró en 1985 que la posibilidad de que Segnosaurus fuera un devorador de peces acuáticos pudiera explicar sus dientes pequeños y puntiagudos y sus pies anchos y quizás palmeados

facts.statement: Segnosaurus belongs to the family Therizinosauridae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Therizinosauridae

facts.statement: Segnosaurus is classified within the class Reptilia.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Segnosaurus is Segnosaurus galbinensis.
facts.quote: Type species: Segnosaurus galbinensis

facts.statement: Segnosaurus lived between 100.5 and 83.6 million years ago during the Cenomanian to Santonian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Cenomanian to Santonian (100.5 to 83.6 million years ago)

facts.statement: There are six recorded fossil occurrences of Segnosaurus in the Paleobiology Database.
facts.quote: Fossil occurrences recorded: 6
